summaries.example: Imagine a box filled with four kinds of building pieces: red, blue, green, and yellow. The pieces never disappear, but they can be mixed into new shapes or pulled apart. Empedocles thought the world worked somewhat like this. His four roots were fire, air, earth, and water. Love helped them join, while Strife helped separate them. A tree, an animal, or a person was a temporary mixture of these lasting roots.
summaries.summary: Empedocles was an ancient Greek philosopher and poet from Acragas in Sicily. He taught that all things are made from four lasting roots: fire, air, earth, and water. Two forces act on them. Love brings different roots together, and Strife separates them. Because the roots themselves never begin or end, change happens when their mixtures change. This let Empedocles explain how a changing world could exist while still accepting the idea that nothing truly comes from nothing or disappears completely. He described a repeating cosmic cycle in which Love and Strife take turns becoming stronger. The same forces help explain the formation of the cosmos, plants, animals, and people. He also suggested that perception works through a likeness between what is outside us and the roots within us, with tiny flows from objects reaching sense organs. Thinking may depend especially on the balanced mixture of roots in blood, although scholars disagree about exactly how perception and thought are related. Empedocles is also associated with a poem traditionally called Purifications. Its fragments describe spirits moving through plants, animals, and humans after wrongdoing, and eventually returning to a divine condition. The poems criticize bloodshed and meat-eating. The surviving evidence is incomplete, so scholars debate the order of Empedocles’ ideas and whether On Nature and Purifications were separate works. His combination of natural explanation, poetry, ethics, and religious ideas influenced later philosophers and writers.
key_ideas: Everything is made from four permanent roots: fire, air, earth, and water.
The roots do not vanish. They join and separate in different mixtures.
Love joins the roots, while Strife pulls them apart.
Empedocles used this picture to explain the world, living things, and some kinds of seeing and thinking.
His poems also taught that living beings should avoid bloodshed and treat life as connected.
Scholars are still unsure whether his surviving pieces came from two poems or one larger project.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empedocles shows that people in the ancient world could ask scientific-sounding questions while also using poetry, religion, and stories about right and wrong. His idea that lasting parts can form changing things influenced later thinking about nature. His work also reminds us that old ideas often survive in fragments, so understanding them requires careful comparison and patience.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher from Acragas in Sicily who explained nature using four basic roots and two powerful forces.
The four lasting ingredients Empedocles said make up everything: fire, air, earth, and water.
The force that brings different roots together and makes mixtures possible.
The force that pulls roots apart and makes separation and breaking apart possible.
A repeating pattern in which Love and Strife take turns becoming stronger.
The idea that a spirit can move through many different living forms over time.

questions_to_think_about: If the same basic parts make everything, what makes one thing different from another?
Can joining and separating explain all the changes we see?
Why might a philosopher connect ideas about nature with rules about how people should live?
What would be difficult about trying to understand a book that survives only in pieces?

summaries.example: Consider a bronze statue. On one description, the statue comes into being when existing material is arranged into a new form; it does not arise from absolute nothing. Empedocles extends this thought to the whole natural world: fire, air, earth, and water are permanent constituents, while Love and Strife explain their changing combinations. A living body would therefore be a temporary, proportioned mixture rather than a wholly new substance. The analogy is limited, however, because Empedocles’ forces are not merely human choices or mechanical pushes: they are active principles that structure the cosmic cycle.
summaries.summary: Empedocles, a fifth-century BCE thinker from Acragas, developed a natural philosophy in hexameter verse. His central ontology contains four everlasting roots—fire, air, earth, and water—and two everlasting powers, Love and Strife. The roots are not inert pieces in a modern mechanical sense; their divine naming suggests active natures. Love attracts unlike roots and produces combination, while Strife separates them. Their strength changes through a recurring cosmic process, but neither power finally eliminates the other. This framework responds to the challenge associated with Parmenides: if genuine coming-to-be and passing-away are impossible, how can the experienced world contain plurality and change? Empedocles answers that the roots remain, while compounds form and dissolve. Interpretations of the cycle diverge. On a traditional reading, a Love-dominated Sphere gives way to separation under Strife, and the reverse movement may contain a second cosmos and generation of living things. Other interpreters find only one cosmogony and zoogony, with the cosmos forming during a movement from separation toward mixture. The fragmentary evidence, including material from the Strasbourg papyrus and later scholia, has not settled the issue. Empedocles’ biology describes mixtures of roots in proportions, unusual early combinations of limbs and bodies, and the formation of ordinary animals and humans. His account of perception uses affinity: external effluences may enter pores in sense organs suited to them. Thinking is associated with the mixture of roots in blood near the heart, although the boundary between perception and cognition is uncertain. key_ideas: Empedocles preserves plurality and change while treating the roots and forces as everlasting. Change is recombination and separation, not absolute creation or destruction.
Love and Strife are not simply emotions. They are cosmic principles whose alternating influence generates the order and history of the world.
Interpretations differ over whether the cosmic cycle contains two cosmogonies and two zoogonies or one of each within a broader cycle.

His account of organisms includes mixtures in definite proportions, strange early forms, and the development of viable creatures; some scholars compare this with an anticipation of evolutionary thinking, but the comparison remains interpretive.
Perception may depend on likeness between internal and external roots, with effluences passing through pores. Cognition may also depend on the elemental mixture of blood around the heart.
The relation between On Nature and Purifications is disputed: they may be separate but connected poems, levels of one teaching, or parts of a more unified project.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empedocles is important because he refuses a simple choice between a world of unchanging being and a world made from absolute beginnings. His roots preserve permanence, while Love and Strife explain process, order, and breakdown. He also illustrates how ancient philosophy crossed boundaries now often drawn between physics, biology, psychology, ethics, poetry, and religion. Since the evidence is partial and its organization disputed, studying Empedocles provides a useful lesson in how philosophical interpretation works: arguments must remain sensitive to uncertainty rather than treating one reconstruction as settled fact.

important_terms.definition: The claim that reality consists of enduring constituents rather than things that come into existence from nothing or are annihilated.
Empedocles’ four basic, enduring constituents: fire, air, earth, and water. He calls them roots and presents them with divine names.
An active principle that attracts unlike roots and produces harmonious mixtures.
An active principle that separates roots and produces division and dissolution.
The account of how an ordered cosmos comes to be from the activity and changing dominance of Love and Strife.
The account of how animals and other living beings come to be.
The idea that a long-lived divine spirit undergoes a series of incarnations in plants, animals, and humans.
Small material flows from objects that, according to one interpretation, reach appropriately shaped openings in sense organs.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining change as recombination solve the problem of how something can come to be without arising from nothing?
What would count as evidence for one cosmic cycle with one creation of living things rather than two?
If perception depends on likeness, how could this account explain qualities such as color or shape?
Can a physical theory of mixtures support ethical obligations against bloodshed, or does that require additional premises?
How should interpreters reason from fragmentary texts when different arrangements produce different philosophical systems?

summaries.example: Suppose you mix blue and yellow paint to make green, then separate the paints again. The colors have not been created from nothing or destroyed forever; they have been combined and divided. Empedocles used a much larger version of this idea. He said that fire, air, earth, and water are always present, but their mixtures change. Love helps different roots cooperate, while Strife makes them pull apart. A body, a plant, or a planet is therefore a temporary arrangement in a much longer cycle.
summaries.summary: Empedocles was a fifth-century BCE philosopher and poet from Acragas, a city in Sicily. His main natural theory says that everything is made from four permanent roots: fire, air, earth, and water. Two forces move them: Love brings different roots into harmony, and Strife drives them apart. The roots and forces do not disappear. Instead, the world changes because the roots combine in different ways. This theory tries to answer a problem raised by Parmenides, who argued that coming into existence and passing away are difficult to make sense of. Empedocles keeps permanence and change together: the basic ingredients remain, while their temporary mixtures are born and destroyed. He describes a cosmic cycle. At one stage, Love unites the roots in a Sphere; at another, Strife separates them. Scholars disagree about the exact order and about whether there are two periods in which a cosmos and living things are formed, or only one. Empedocles’ account of living things includes mixtures of the roots, unusual early bodies made from wandering limbs, and the later emergence of familiar animals and humans. Some readers see a resemblance to evolution, but the entry presents this as an interpretation, not a settled fact. Empedocles also explains perception through likeness. Things send out tiny flows, and sense organs may receive flows that fit their openings. Thought seems connected to the mixture of roots in blood around the heart, though it is unclear whether he sharply separates thinking from sensing. A second group of fragments, traditionally called Purifications, describes spirits falling into a long cycle of plant, animal, and human lives after wrongdoing. key_ideas: Empedocles thought the four roots and the two forces always existed.
What we call birth and death are changes in combination: roots come together or separate.
Love and Strife work against each other, but neither wins forever.
He used the same basic theory to discuss the cosmos, living creatures, perception, and thought.
His moral teaching connected purification with avoiding bloodshed and meat-eating.
Researchers disagree about how to arrange the surviving fragments and whether they came from two poems or one connected work.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empedocles matters because he offered a broad picture of reality rather than a theory about only one subject. His ideas connect physical change with living things, perception, thought, and ethical behavior. He also shows why historical philosophy must be handled carefully: much of his work is lost, later reports may be unreliable, and the surviving pieces can support more than one thoughtful interpretation.

important_terms.definition: An ancient Greek thinker and poet from Acragas, in Sicily, who developed a theory of four basic roots and two cosmic forces.
Empedocles’ name for the basic, permanent constituents of everything: fire, air, earth, and water.
The force that attracts unlike roots and combines them into organized mixtures.
The force that separates roots and breaks mixtures apart.
A repeating history of the universe in which Love and Strife take turns having greater influence.
The study or explanation of how the universe becomes an ordered world.
The explanation of how animals and other living things develop.
The belief that a spirit or daemon passes through a series of living bodies.

questions_to_think_about: How is Empedocles’ explanation of change different from saying that things appear from nothing?
Why might Love need Strife, rather than simply defeating it?
Would a mixture of four roots be enough to explain why a person can think?
How might fragmentary evidence lead reasonable scholars to different conclusions?
What changes when a theory of nature is also used to guide human behavior?
